conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days; it helps us spot signs of postpartum depression or anxiety so we can offer the right support. Everything you share stays confidential between you and our care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question.

Over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[slow exhale, small shrug]  
I still laugh sometimes—like when my partner makes a goofy face at the baby—but it feels… flatter? I’d say most days I can chuckle once or twice, just not as easily as before she was born.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, like I said, I can still laugh—maybe once a day—but it’s not that full-on belly laugh I used to have. It feels kind of forced or muted most of the time.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[sighs softly, eyes down]  
I do look forward to little things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my morning coffee—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. I’d say sometimes I look forward to stuff, but not as often or as much as before.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[shoulders slump a little]  
Yeah… when she wouldn’t settle last night I kept thinking, “Maybe my milk isn’t good enough” or “I must be missing something.” I know it’s probably not really my fault, but those thoughts still pop in—maybe every other day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly worry her breathing sounds different—even though she’s fine. It happens maybe a couple of times a day, but I can usually calm myself down pretty quickly.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky, but once or twice I’ve felt this quick wave of “what if something bad happens?”—like when she cried harder than usual. My heart races for a minute, then it passes. It’s not an everyday thing, though.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like yesterday—she wouldn’t nap, laundry was piled up, and I felt I couldn’t keep up. I got that tight-chest feeling and thought, “How will I manage everything?” It passes once I tick off one small task, but it hits maybe a few times a week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that bad. I do get sad sometimes, but I can still fall asleep pretty easily. Maybe once or twice I’ve tossed and turned for a bit when I’m stressed, but mostly I’m out once my head hits the pillow.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes flick down, voice softer]  
Yeah… I do feel sad some days. Not the whole day, just moments—like this morning when I couldn’t get her to smile during tummy time. I’d say most days there’s at least a little patch where I feel down, but it lifts after a while.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Maybe once or twice this week. Yesterday I just sat on the couch with her asleep on me and felt overwhelmed—tears came for a minute or two, then I wiped them away and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I could never do that to my baby or my family.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 4–6 weeks post-delivery; reports intact social supports; breast-feeding.

1. Presenting symptoms endorsed  
- Depressed mood: “sad some days… at least a little patch” (Q8)  
- Reduced pleasure/interest: muted laughter, decreased anticipatory enjoyment (Q1, Q2)  
- Episodic tearfulness: 1–2 x/week (Q9)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt: every-other-day thoughts of inadequacy (Q3)  
- Anxiety: daily non-specific worries; occasional brief “heart-racing” episodes; 2–3 x/week feeling overwhelmed (Q4, Q5, Q6)  
- No self-harm ideation (Q10)  
- Sleep remains generally intact (Q7)

2. Pattern summary  
Persistent low mood with reduced enjoyment, mild-moderate anxiety, and situational tearfulness since delivery; no current safety concerns.

3. Screening significance  
Meets some criteria for possible postpartum depression (mood, anhedonia, guilt, crying) and generalized anxiety (daily worries, tension). No current suicidality.

4. Risk factors noted  
- Primiparity  
- Self-reported “can’t keep up” episodes  
- No prior mental-health history reported

5. Next steps (screening only)  
Recommend formal clinical interview (EPDS or PHQ-9) and assessment of functional impairment; consider referral for perinatal mental-health services; educate on emergency resources if symptoms worsen or safety concerns develop.

Clinician: [signature]
